body_markdown:
Playing with cars, especially when you’re trying to make one better, often involves tradeoffs. That’s especially true if you engage in the old-car hobby with less than an *anything goes!* checking account. And even if you are that flush, in order to properly tweak a vehicle to, say, handle like a race car, you may well end up with a ride that makes every pothole feel like you’re driving on a bombing range. We even found[some guy with a Bugatti Bolide](https://www.facebook.com/reel/2474939486369161) who’s annoyed that it lacks a suitable ashtray. Learn to compromise a little, Smokey, like the rest of us!


When it comes to project cars, it’s smart to balance your potential compromises well ahead of time. Prioritizing one aspect of the project does not necessarily mean you must bail on the others, but it can help you decide how much time, effort and money you want to invest in lower-on-the-list priorities that might contribute less to your project’s intended mission.


You *do* have a realistic expectation regarding the intended use of you project car, correct? And a realistic road map to reach that destination? I’d submit that having a plan saved me a lot of time and frustration on my pending Chevrolet Corvette C4 project, but drawing up that map meant making some hard decisions regarding priorities: What was important enough to deserve a healthy allocation of my time and money, and what wasn’t?


In the end,[my answer boiled down to](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/my-corvette-will-be-right-the-first-time-regardless-of-time/) listing three major tradeoffs for the Corvette.


## Trade-off 1: The Right Parts, but a Lot of Work


Jordan Lewis


As you plan out most projects, you’ll likely find as I did that many of the parts and pieces my tired Corvette needs are served up in several different flavors. One metal under-hood part I expect to buy is available from a hitherto-unknown, way-overseas distributor, and may have been crafted from discarded beer cans. Down the aisle, a kind-of comparable part is served up by a company we’ve all done business with, and their product is a machined-billet work of art that could solve my problem almost as quickly as it would drain my wallet.


An example: In order to afford the Dorman LS2 intake manifold I want, I chose to pass up engine dress-up bling like ribbed valve covers or a sparkling accessory drive. Sure, I’ll take the time to clean and paint the original-equipment items to make them presentable as possible, but I spent my money where it would make the most difference in the final product. I also invested the time to find parts that accomplished my goals but were not saddled with the sort of “popularity tax” that is aimed at some LS engine parts. Sure, it would have been nice to have a set of number 823 cylinder heads, but the 706 heads I got for a fraction of the price get me the same compression, and comparable flow. I’ll still reach my power goals, and I can continue to use cathedral-port accessories, which are a bit more affordable than those with rectangle porting.


## Trade-off 2: No Flash, All Reliability


Jordan Lewis


Sure, there are plenty of ways to make a big project like this look and feel unique, using custom one-off parts or some artful combination of existing parts. Just look at the[vehicles featured at SEMA](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/sema/) : I did, and then I ran the other way. Not because they are bad, because they aren’t. But I am more interested in a reliable and trustworthy build, even if people might consider it boring. Sure, I enjoy building a car while I’m actually *building* it, but once it’s done, I’m done. I don’t want to have to worry about finding replacements for rare, one-off parts that could interrupt my road trip, or even just a drive around town.


This typically means[sticking to the KISS method](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/breaking-my-corvette-has-changed-my-plans-for-the-project/) for a build. And if we can add a cliche: If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. Fancy kits or custom bits may only mean headaches down the road. My plan is to *drive* this car, not work on it. I already have over 2000 miles on the powertrain swap, and I drove it for the first time just six months ago. My decision to stay with factory-style brakes rather than upgrade to aftermarket units fits my philosophy. The parts are available, and stock brakes are appropriate for what I do with the car, so why spend more on something else I don’t need?


## Trade-off 3: More Go than Show


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


There are plenty of parts available for the C4 to make it much nicer inside and out, but few of them interest me. After all, this is not a restoration. It’s just an old car we’ve built for having fun, to teach us, to bring together a group of friends. The engine, transmission and the choice of rear axle ratios conspire to make the car quicker than it has any right to be, but looking at it when street-parked, you’d have no idea. When I recently drove the Corvette to a morning car show, I overheard someone saying, “You’d think he would have at least washed it.”


Perhaps. But it’s freeing to not much care what the old Corvette looks like, so long as it starts when I turn the key. And the way it responds when I press the skinny pedal can be downright addicting. I used to think I didn’t care about how my other cars looked, and it turns that’s not true. The perspective I’ve gained owning this car has taken me to a place where I’ve realized that my 1965 Corvair is actually a blend of form and function. With this Corvette, I’ve focused on just the function, and it made the build come together quicker and easier, and it was much simpler to map out.


These were just three of the compromises that I consciously decided were worth it; your mileage may vary. Before you start a project, unless you are planning to build a concours-winner, a race winner or a comfortable daily driver—or all three—think about trade-offs you may need to make, so you end up with a build that you can finish on time, on budget, and delivers the sort of fun we’ve had with our Corvette.


Project cars are seldom easy, but any trip seems more satisfying when you have a clear map to follow.
